corpus_definition: A natural substance in food that keeps you healthy.

forms.definition: a natural substance in food that your body needs to stay healthy
forms.example: Oranges are full of vitamin C.
forms.note: British: /ˈvɪtəmɪn/; American: /ˈvaɪtəmɪn/.

syn.note: Related: any substance in food that helps you grow and stay healthy; vitamins are one kind of nutrient.
Related: iron and calcium are minerals, not vitamins, but both are needed for good health.
Related: a pill or drink you take to get extra vitamins or other things your body needs.

forms.note: There is no verb made from vitamin.
There is no common adjective made from vitamin. Vital (very important) shares an old root but is not made from vitamin.
There is no adverb made from vitamin.

context.text: My grandmother in Fergana says apricots are full of vitamins. In winter, when there is less fresh fruit, she gives us vitamin C tablets.

reviewer_note: Two corpus rows with the same meaning merged. vital listed as not_family (shared Latin root only).

corpus_definition: someone who works without pay to help other people

forms.definition: a person who works without pay to help other people
forms.example: She is a volunteer at the local hospital.

syn.note: Close, but it does not show that the person chose to help.
Related: anyone who helps; a helper may be paid or not.

forms.definition: to offer to do something without being asked or paid
forms.example: Every summer, students volunteer to clean the parks in Tashkent.

syn.note: Offer is general; volunteer usually means doing it for free or by your own choice.
Related: to offer help or information, often when people are asked.

ant.note: To say no when you are asked to do something.

forms.definition: done because you choose to do it, not because you must
forms.example: The extra English lessons are voluntary, but most students come.
forms.note: Voluntary work = work done without pay. Same family: volunteer was made from the French form of voluntary.

syn.note: Optional means you can choose; voluntary also suggests you want to do it.
Related: voluntary work is usually unpaid.
Related: describes a person who is happy to do something.

ant.note: Something you must do because of a rule or law.
Formal word for something you must do.

forms.definition: because you choose to, not because someone makes you
forms.example: He left the job voluntarily to start his own business.

syn.note: Willingly also shows that you are happy to do it.
Related: without anyone controlling or forcing you.
Easy everyday phrase with almost the same meaning.

context.text: Aziza volunteers at a children's library in Samarkand every Saturday. The work is voluntary, so she gets no money, but she says being a volunteer makes her happy.

reviewer_note: Headword is itself a person noun, so it stays the main noun entry (rule 6). voluntary/voluntarily kept as family (volunteer is made from voluntary).

corpus_definition: a long journey, especially by sea

forms.definition: a long journey, especially by ship or in space
forms.example: The voyage across the Atlantic took three weeks.

syn.note: Journey is general; a voyage is usually long and by sea or in space.
Easy phrase with the same meaning.
Related: a trip across a sea, lake or river, often a short one.
Related: a holiday on a large ship that stops at different places.
Related: a trip is usually shorter and for fun or work.

forms.definition: to travel a long way, especially by sea
forms.example: The explorers voyaged across the ocean to find new lands.

syn.note: Sail is common and always about boats or ships.
Related: travel is the everyday word for any journey.

forms.note: There is no adjective made from voyage.
There is no adverb made from voyage.

people.definition: a person who goes on a long journey, especially by sea
people.example: The early voyagers had only the stars to guide them.

context.text: In the past, a voyage from Europe to Asia could take months. Voyagers carried food and water for the whole trip, because there were few ports on the way.

reviewer_note: Verb voyage and voyager are real but literary; marked with register. Uzbekistan has no sea, so the context is historical.

corpus_definition: The regular money paid to a person for their labor.

forms.definition: the money a worker gets every week or for each hour of work
forms.example: He receives a weekly wage for his labor.
forms.note: Often plural: 'Wages are low in this factory.' Minimum wage = the lowest pay the law allows.

syn.note: Everyday word for money you get for working.
A salary is paid every month or year, usually for office or professional jobs; a wage is often paid weekly or by the hour.
All the money you get from working, sometimes from more than one job.
Related: all the money you get, including from rent or business, not only from work.

forms.definition: to start and continue a war or a fight against something
forms.example: The city is waging a campaign against dirty streets.
forms.note: Belongs to wage = carry on a war or campaign (wage war), not money for work. Formal.
There is no common adjective made from wage. British English has the rare formal words waged and unwaged (having / not having paid work).
There is no adverb made from wage.

context.text: My brother works in a shop in Bukhara and gets his wage every Friday. He says the wages are better in Tashkent, so he may move there next year.

reviewer_note: Two rows with the same meaning merged. Verb wage (wage war) is other_meaning. waged/unwaged kept in a note only (rare, formal British). wage earner is a compound, left out.

corpus_definition: To walk around slowly without a clear goal or path.

forms.definition: a slow walk around a place, just for pleasure
forms.example: Let's go for a wander around the old town.
forms.note: Mostly British English: go for / have a wander.

syn.note: A slow, relaxed walk; very close.
General word; a wander has no fixed direction.

forms.definition: to walk around slowly with no clear purpose or direction
forms.example: They decided to wander through the quiet city streets.
forms.note: Don't confuse with wonder (to think about something).

syn.note: Easy phrase; it does not always show that you have no plan.
Walk slowly and calmly, usually for pleasure.
Move around a large area without a plan, often for a long time.
Related: move slowly without control, like a boat on water.

ant.note: To move fast because you need to be somewhere.

forms.definition: moving from place to place and not staying anywhere for long
forms.example: A wandering dog followed us home.

syn.note: Very close; moving around a wide area.
Related: moving from place to place. American spelling: traveling.
Related: has no home; used for people and animals.

ant.note: Living in one place for a long time.

forms.note: There is no adverb made from wander.

people.definition: a person who travels from place to place without a home or a plan
people.example: The old wanderer stopped at our village for one night.

context.text: On Sunday we wandered around the Chorsu Bazaar with no plan at all. A wandering cat followed us from stall to stall, and after our long wander we were hungry.

reviewer_note: Spelling trap: wander vs wonder flagged in the verb note. Noun wander marked informal (mostly British).

corpus_definition: To tell someone about a possible danger.

forms.definition: something that tells you about a possible danger or problem
forms.example: There was a warning on the radio about strong winds.

syn.note: A quick message about danger, often from a phone or the news.
Related: being careful; also a formal warning, for example from the police.
Related: written information that tells people something, not always about danger.

forms.definition: to tell someone that something bad or dangerous may happen
forms.example: I tried to warn him about the ice.
forms.note: Patterns: warn someone about/of something; warn someone (not) to do something.

syn.note: Tell someone quickly about danger so they can act.
More formal: tell someone to be careful.
Related: tell someone what you think they should do, not always about danger.
Related: very general; warn always means telling about danger.

forms.note: There is no real adjective made from warn. In 'warning sign' or 'warning light', warning is a noun used before another noun.
There is no common adverb made from warn; warningly is very rare.

context.text: The weather service warned people in Tashkent about a dust storm. After the warning, many parents kept their children at home.

reviewer_note: Two rows with the same meaning merged. Adjective slot is no_form: 'warning' before a noun is attributive noun use.

forms.definition: the quality of being very strange or unusual
forms.example: Everyone noticed the weirdness of his behaviour that day.

syn.note: Same meaning; a little more neutral.
Close; slightly less strong.

ant.note: The state of being normal. American English often uses normalcy.

forms.note: There is no single-word verb made from weird. Informal English has the phrasal verb weird out ('That film weirded me out').

forms.definition: very strange or unusual, and sometimes hard to understand
forms.example: That is a very weird color for a car.
forms.note: Spelling trap: e before i (weird), not 'wierd'.

syn.note: Neutral word with the same meaning.
Close, but a little less strong.
Stronger: very strange and surprising.
Related: not common; it can be good or bad.

ant.note: Not special or different in any way.

forms.definition: in a very strange or unusual way
forms.example: The street was weirdly quiet for a Saturday night.

syn.note: Same meaning, more neutral.
Close, a little less strong.

ant.note: In the usual or expected way.

people.definition: a person who behaves in a very strange way
people.example: Some kids called him a weirdo, but he didn't care.
people.note: Can be rude; use with care.

context.text: Last night I heard a weird noise in the kitchen. The house was weirdly quiet after that, so I turned on all the lights.

reviewer_note: weirdo marked informal and possibly rude. weird out (phrasal) mentioned in the verb note only.

corpus_definition: The skills and knowledge you gained from past jobs.
usage_note: Uncountable noun: 'have work experience', 'relevant / previous work experience' (not 'a work experience'). In British English it also means a short time when a student works somewhere to learn about a job: 'do work experience at a bank'.

relations.note: In job adverts 'experience' alone usually means work experience.
Related: your past education and jobs together.
Related: what you have done well (or badly) in the past.
Related: a period of work, often for students, to get work experience.

context.text: Many companies in Tashkent ask for at least two years of work experience. Dilnoza got her first work experience at a bank while she was still at university.

reviewer_note: Fixed noun phrase; uncountable use and the British school sense noted.

corpus_definition: A series of exercises done to get fit.

forms.definition: a period of physical exercise that you do to stay fit and strong
forms.example: I feel great after my morning workout.

syn.note: General word; a workout is one planned session of exercise.
Often used for sports teams and athletes.
Related: regular exercise over a long time to prepare for a sport.

forms.note: No single-word verb. The verb is the phrasal verb work out (two words): 'I work out at the gym three times a week.'
There is no adjective made from workout.
There is no adverb made from workout.

context.text: Every morning before university, Jasur does a short workout in the park. His sister prefers to work out at the gym in the evening.

reviewer_note: Noun is one word (workout); the verb is two words (work out). Verb slot is no_form with that note.

corpus_definition: The office or building where you do your job.

forms.definition: the office, factory or other building where people do their jobs
forms.example: Safety is important in every workplace.

syn.note: Same meaning, a little more formal.
Related: one kind of workplace, with desks and computers.
Everyday English: 'I'm at work' often means 'I'm at my workplace'.

forms.note: There is no verb made from workplace.
There is no adjective made from workplace.
There is no adverb made from workplace.

context.text: A good workplace has clean air and friendly people. In our workplace in Namangan, everyone eats lunch together on Fridays.

reviewer_note: Headword is itself a compound; no family forms.
